title: Rama's vow of refuge
hookLine: the enemy's brother asks to be let in; the camp argues; Rama vows refuge to anyone who comes
carry: sharanagati: whoever comes once is held

cards: A war camp on a beach, the eve of battle. A figure appears in the sky above it, with four armed companions, and calls down: I'm the enemy king's brother, please let me in. Sugriva, king of the monkeys, doesn't hesitate.
He goes straight to Rama: this is a trick. He's a rakshasa, Ravana's own brother, and he'll strike when we're not looking. Kill him, or send him away.

teach.b: Rama asks his council, and Valmiki lets every voice speak. Angada says test him first. Others say send a spy, or question him closely.
Then Hanuman speaks, the one who has actually been inside Lanka. He came openly, not in disguise. I've watched his face, and I see no deceit in it.
Accept him. Then Rama gives his answer. I can't turn away someone who comes as a friend, even if he has faults.

teach.h: ANYONE WHO SAYS I AM YOURS.
teach.b: Anyone who comes to me even once and says, I am yours, I give safety from every being. That is my vow. Sugriva still pushes back.
Rama goes further. Even if it were Ravana himself, bring him in.
In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, this verse is treasured as a teaching on sharanagati, taking refuge in God: the one who turns to God even once, sincerely, is held.
Others read it more plainly, as the code of a good king toward someone asking for protection.

teach.h: KING OF LANKA, ON THE BEACH.
teach.b: Then Rama has Vibhishana come down, sends for sea water, and pours it over his head, consecrating him king of Lanka, right there on the beach, before a single battle has been fought.

teach.h: EVEN IF IT WERE RAVANA HIMSELF.
teach.b: That vow is why so many Hindus aren't afraid to come back to the shrine after years away: by Rama's own word, one sincere turning is enough.
And Sugriva's question is still asked today, at lunch tables and family dinners, whenever someone who hurt us asks to come back: what if it's a trick? Rama never calls the caution foolish.
He just says the refuge is bigger.

how: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition the Vibhishana episode is taught as the model of śaraṇāgati, taking refuge, and Rama's vow in Yuddha Kanda 18 is recited and commented on as a central verse.

games.q: a cousin who hasn't been to the temple in ten years asks nani if it's too late to start again. by Rama's vow, what fits?
o: it's not too late: one sincere turning, and you're held.
first prove it by coming every week for a year.
only if they never once stopped believing.
games.why: Rama vows safety to anyone who comes even once and says i am yours. Sri Vaishnavas call this sharanagati, taking refuge.

practice: Fold your hands, the way Hindus do at every shrine. Say quietly, once, Rama, I am yours, and mean it as much as you can today. Then breathe slowly and rest in the vow: once is enough.
If you don't pray, keep your hands folded and think of someone asking to come back to you, and let the door open one inch.

wordCard.voice: Vibhishana's crossing. The enemy's brother asks for refuge, the camp argues, and Rama vows safety to anyone who comes even once and says, I am yours.

orig.note: Sanskrit śaraṇāgati: coming for refuge, from śaraṇa, refuge or shelter, and āgati, arrival; a key word in Sri Vaishnava teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: sharanagati, whoever comes once is held. Tomorrow, two spies are caught in the camp. Day six hundred thirty-eight, done.
